clue.text: Deformed, incestuous, patricidal, blind

parts.note: a list of the traits of the Theban king of Greek legend: his name means swollen foot, he married his mother, killed his father and blinded himself

explanation.surface: A grim catalogue of a tragic figure's afflictions and crimes.
explanation.walkthrough: Each adjective fits the legendary king of Thebes: lamed as a baby (his name means 'swollen foot'), wed to his mother, slayer of his father, self-blinded. The answer is the adjective formed from his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything belonging to or resembling the Theban king of Sophocles' tragedy, whose story holds all four traits.

clue.text: What Benchley and Parker had in common

definitions.text: What Benchley and Parker had in common

parts.words: What Benchley and Parker had in common
parts.note: the humorists Robert Benchley and Dorothy Parker famously shared a tiny workroom at Vanity Fair

explanation.surface: A question about two American wits and what united them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In common' suggests a shared trait or friendship, but the shared thing is literal: a room they worked in together. Parker quipped that it was so small that one cubic foot less and it would have been adultery.
explanation.definitionFit: Benchley and Parker literally shared a workroom, a place of business, at the magazine.

clue.text: Eliot character drawn from Calderón dated 1876

indicators.note: the letters are pulled out of the run of words that follows, as a picture is drawn from life

explanation.surface: A George Eliot figure modelled on the Spanish dramatist, with a date attached.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel Deronda is George Eliot's last novel, published in 1876, which the clue's date confirms. The letters run across the end of 'Calderón' and the start of 'dated'.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel, the title figure of George Eliot's last novel, bears this surname.

clue.text: Dramatists' Sicilian prince apparently likes michaelmas daisy but associated with love lies a-bleeding

parts.note: phil- is the Greek-derived element meaning loving or liking, as in philanthropy
a michaelmas daisy is a kind of aster, the autumn-flowering plant

explanation.surface: A theatrical prince described through garden flowers, one of which is called love-lies-bleeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' signals that the name only seems to break this way. The play by Beaumont and Fletcher is subtitled 'Love Lies a-Bleeding', which the last words point to; love-lies-bleeding is also a garden plant, keeping up the flower theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Philaster is the title hero, heir to Sicily, of a play by the dramatists Beaumont and Fletcher.

clue.text: Mrs George Wickham

parts.note: in Pride and Prejudice the officer Wickham elopes with and then marries the youngest Bennet sister

explanation.walkthrough: The married name points back to the maiden name: in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice the youngest Bennet sister runs off with Wickham and marries him.
explanation.definitionFit: In Austen's novel, the youngest of the five Bennet sisters becomes Wickham's wife after eloping.

clue.text: Delmar Schwartz work preceding success of Leon Uris

definitions.meaning: the American poet Delmore Schwartz published a long poem with this biblical title in 1943
Leon Uris's bestseller was Exodus, and in the Bible the book before Exodus is this one

explanation.surface: Two American writers' books set side by side in order of publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preceding' means the book that comes before in the Bible: Uris's hit novel was Exodus, so the answer is the first book of the Old Testament. The poet's first name is Delmore.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses name the first book of the Bible: a title Schwartz borrowed, and the book that precedes Exodus.

clue.text: Greene had one to sell

parts.note: Graham Greene's 1936 thriller is titled A ... for Sale

explanation.surface: A novelist with merchandise to sell.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's thriller 'A Gun for Sale' supplies the item he had to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's 1936 novel has a firearm for sale in its title, so the novelist had one to sell.

clue.text: Mrs Buck's mother?

parts.note: the novelist Pearl Buck's first name is Pearl, so her mother would be mother-of-pearl

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Buck is the novelist Pearl S. Buck; a pearl's mother is mother-of-pearl, the iridescent shell lining.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl is the iridescent lining of shells, and the novelist's first name was Pearl.

clue.text: "None can drive him from the envious plea / Of forfeiture, of justice, and his bond", he warned

definitions.text: "None can drive him from the envious plea / Of forfeiture, of justice, and his bond", he warned

parts.words: "None can drive him from the envious plea / Of forfeiture, of justice, and his bond", he warned
parts.note: lines from The Merchant of Venice, Act 3, spoken of Shylock by one of Antonio's friends

explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice, Act 3 Scene 2, Antonio's friend reports that Shylock will insist on his bond; the speaker is this minor character.
explanation.definitionFit: These lines belong to Antonio's friend in Shakespeare's Venetian comedy, warning that Shylock will insist on his forfeit.

clue.text: Warship convenience in subordinate divisions

parts.note: a sub, short for submarine, is a naval vessel
the heads are a ship's lavatory, and a convenience is a polite word for a toilet

explanation.surface: Toilets on a naval vessel found in lesser sections.
explanation.walkthrough: A public convenience in British usage is a lavatory; on board ship the lavatory is the heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Subheads are the lesser headings that split a text into its smaller sections.

clue.text: Out of bounds, like Wheatley's territory

definitions.meaning: an area out of bounds is one you are not allowed to enter
Dennis Wheatley's first novel was The ... Territory, 1933

explanation.surface: A no-go area compared with a thriller writer's setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Dennis Wheatley's 1933 thriller 'The Forbidden Territory' supplies the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of bounds means prohibited, and Wheatley's novel is titled with the same prohibited word.

clue.text: Godwin's flawed hero of Falkland's

parts.note: in William Godwin's novel the title character is secretary to the squire Falkland and uncovers his crime

explanation.walkthrough: William Godwin's 1794 novel 'Caleb Williams' follows a secretary in the service of the squire Falkland; the answer is the hero's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: William Godwin's 1794 novel is named after its narrator, Falkland's secretary, whose first name this is.

clue.text: Roman poet a transgressor, we hear

indicators.note: says that the word for a transgressor is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a sinner is one who transgresses moral law

explanation.surface: A poet of ancient Rome branded a wrongdoer by rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech 'sinner' sounds like the name. Shakespeare's Julius Caesar has a Cinna the poet torn apart by a mob that mistakes him for the conspirator.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius Helvius Cinna was a Roman poet, a friend of Catullus.

clue.text: An early victim of Washington found touching by Mark Twain?

definitions.text: An early victim of Washington found touching by Mark Twain?

parts.words: An early victim of Washington found touching by Mark Twain?
parts.note: the legend has young George Washington cutting down a fruit tree and confessing; the query points to a version where Twain retells it with a different tree

explanation.walkthrough: The Parson Weems legend has young George Washington felling his father's tree and admitting it; the familiar version names a cherry, and the question mark allows the setter's tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit tree was the boy Washington's legendary victim of the hatchet.

clue.text: Curiously help is offered to house large chamber group in Sophocles tragedy

indicators.note: one set of letters gives a home to the other, which goes inside it
the letters of 'help is' are arranged in a curious, unexpected order

parts.note: an octet, eight players, is a large ensemble for chamber music

explanation.surface: Assistance arrives to accommodate a big ensemble for a Greek play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curiously' signals the anagram and 'to house' the container; 'is offered' reads as a link, though its 'is' joins the letters to rearrange. Sophocles' play concerns the archer marooned on Lemnos.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles' play is named after the archer abandoned on Lemnos with Heracles' bow.

clue.text: Trollope's description of chessman at site of Hampton Court?

parts.note: a castle is the familiar name for the rook in chess
Hampton Court Palace lies in the London borough of Richmond upon Thames

explanation.surface: A novelist describing a chess piece at a royal palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampton Court is the Tudor palace on the Thames in the London borough of Richmond upon Thames. Trollope's 1860 novel is set in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Castle Richmond is an 1860 novel by Anthony Trollope, so 'Trollope's' stands for one of his books.

clue.text: Composer of operas hid them in error

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are set down in error, in the wrong order

explanation.walkthrough: 'In error' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is part of the letters to rearrange and 'error' alone signals the anagram. Paul Hindemith wrote operas such as Mathis der Maler.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Hindemith, the German composer, wrote Mathis der Maler and Cardillac among other stage works.

clue.text: "Democracy substitutes — by the incompetent many for appointment by the corrupt few" (Shaw)

definitions.text: "Democracy substitutes — by the incompetent many for appointment by the corrupt few" (Shaw)

parts.words: "Democracy substitutes — by the incompetent many for appointment by the corrupt few" (Shaw)
parts.note: Shaw's maxim in Man and Superman, with the missing word being the choosing of officials by vote

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank from Bernard Shaw's 'Maxims for Revolutionists' in Man and Superman: democracy replaces appointment with choice by vote.
explanation.definitionFit: Choosing by popular vote is what democracy puts in place of appointment by a few.

clue.text: Innocent convocation with great name

parts.note: Pope Innocent III called the great church assembly of 1215 at the Roman basilica of St John

explanation.walkthrough: 'Innocent' is Pope Innocent III, who summoned the Fourth such council in 1215, held at the papal cathedral in Rome; the council is often called the Great one.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1215 church assembly called by Innocent III was held at the Lateran basilica and became known as the Great Council.

clue.text: We shall hear from it, said Tomlinson

definitions.text: We shall hear from it, said Tomlinson

parts.words: We shall hear from it, said Tomlinson
parts.note: points to the call of the Last Judgement, as in Kipling's poem Tomlinson about a soul at heaven's gate

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem 'Tomlinson' is about a dead man's soul at the gates of Heaven and Hell; the Last Judgement is announced by this instrument's call.
explanation.definitionFit: The last call heard at the Day of Judgement comes from this brass instrument.

clue.text: Untried, inept action of Faulkner's eponymous character

indicators.note: badly done or clumsy, so the letters of 'Untried' are handled out of order

explanation.surface: A clumsy, inexperienced novice in a William Faulkner story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inept' signals the anagram of UNTRIED. Faulkner's novel 'Intruder in the Dust' names its title figure by what he does.
explanation.definitionFit: Faulkner's 1948 novel names its title figure as one who breaks in, and this verb is that figure's action.

clue.text: Chat from the Tatler, so to speak

definitions.meaning: the Tatler was Steele's 18th-century periodical, and a tattler is someone who spreads tittle-tattle

explanation.surface: Talk that comes out of a society magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tatler, Richard Steele's periodical of 1709, takes its name from a tattler, one who spreads rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Chat in the sense of idle talk, and a tattler is a person who spreads rumours.

clue.text: Sudden seizure due to pact being torn up

indicators.note: an agreement torn up is destroyed, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A power grab follows the shredding of an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being torn up' rearranges DUE TO PACT; 'seizure' is the taking of power, not a medical fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden, often violent seizure of state power by a small group.

clue.text: Academic who includes archaic pronoun is most senior

indicators.note: one piece takes the other in, enclosing it

parts.note: a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge
ye is the old form of you

explanation.surface: A university teacher uses old-fashioned speech and is the longest-serving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who includes' signals the container. In British usage a don is a lecturer at Oxford or Cambridge, so 'Academic' is not an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: The doyen of a group is its oldest or longest-serving member, the senior figure.

clue.text: Vivaldi's was harmonious

parts.note: Vivaldi's set of concertos is titled L'... armonico, harmonious inspiration

explanation.walkthrough: Vivaldi's Op. 3 is 'L'estro armonico', 'harmonic inspiration'; the answer is the Italian word for inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for poetic inspiration or creative fire, the noun in the title of Vivaldi's Op. 3 concertos.

clue.text: Suggest mischief-maker extremely literary

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite or child

indicators.note: the extremes of the word, its first and last letters, are taken

explanation.surface: A request to hint that a troublemaker is very bookish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'literary', L and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest something is to hint at it without stating it outright.

clue.text: Goings-on at the palace recorded by D'Urfey

definitions.text: Goings-on at the palace recorded by D'Urfey

parts.words: Goings-on at the palace recorded by D'Urfey
parts.note: Thomas D'Urfey's 1697 comedy was titled The ... at Versailles

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas D'Urfey wrote the comedy 'The Intrigues at Versailles' (1697); the palace is Versailles.
explanation.definitionFit: Plots and secret schemes are the goings-on of a court, as in D'Urfey's title.

clue.text: Mountain princess in a state

definitions.meaning: Mount ..., in Crete or near Troy, is a mountain of Greek myth
the title figure of Tennyson's The Princess and of Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess ...
the letters begin the name of the US state Idaho

explanation.walkthrough: Three senses: the mountain of Greek myth, Gilbert and Sullivan's princess, and the first three letters of Idaho.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek mountain, a Gilbert and Sullivan heroine, and the start of the state name Idaho all share these letters.

clue.text: Special observations, not with article

parts.note: and means together with
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Particular remarks made without a definite thing attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' is taken as written, 'with' gives AND and 'article' gives A.
explanation.definitionFit: Notanda is Latin for things to be noted, special remarks set down for attention.
